story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I’m Jason Thomas, one of the founders of CoScreen.

As some of you may know, Datadog sunset the CoScreen service on July 31st.

Four of us from the original CoScreen team have spent the last couple months building a free and open source pair programming tool inspired by those that came before us: It’s called Petal (https://github.com/kiruna-labs/petal)

Some history first, because when we started CoScreen we had hoped to break the sad and established pattern of this industry.

Screenhero was an exceptional tool that a lot of us loved for pairing. Multiple cursors, low latency, you could click your partner’s editor, and just start typing. It felt like magic while we had it. Then Slack bought it in 2015, and shut down the standalone app in December 2017.

When Till, Max, and I started CoScreen, we were aware of this history, and wanted to build an even more magical collaboration and screen sharing experience: the entire concept was “throw a window from your laptop up on someone else’s screen, and start collaborating with zero friction.”

Datadog acquired us in 2022, and thus began the great adventure of adapting our real-time technology into Datadog products, while also continue developing CoScreen as a standalone tool from the Datadog ecosystem. Datadog invested in the product for years and we’re thankful for that. But CoScreen itself proved, like so many other screen sharing tool acquisitions, to be too tangential from the customer base and core mission. We instead built other communication features in Datadog, the integrations with other video platforms, and also its wildly successful MCP server. We weren't the only ones. Around was bought by Miro and shut down in March 2025. Multi (formerly Remotion) was acqui-hired by OpenAI in 2024 and shut down about a month later. It's nearly always the same story: a small team builds something hard that people love, a platform buys it for the team or the feature, and the standalone product doesn't survive the integration. So we decided firmly to do things differently this time. Petal is completely free and open source and we aren't monetizing it. If we lose interest or get hit by a bus, you can self-host it or fork it, and nobody can sunset it on you. Honestly it's a love letter to everyone in this community that supported us, believed in us, and to liberate collaborative screen sharing from this vicious cycle.

We hope through this we can help foster a large and vibrant community around innovating in this product sector. What Petal does: shared windows show up as real windows on your desktop, movable and resizable, not tiles in a grid. Several people can share at once, everyone gets a labeled cursor, and you can click into any shared window to type and scroll. Rooms are persistent, so you click once to join "eng-sync" instead of passing links around. It runs on macOS and Windows (Linux is next, this time for real and you can help us!), plus a web app. Media goes over LiveKit. You can use our hosted instance with zero config, or point the app at your own LiveKit server with one docker-compose if you want the traffic to stay on your network or even use an entirely different video backend if you want to. The part that still feels strange to us: CoScreen took almost six years to build. The first version of Petal took under eight weeks, from scratch, with frontier models like Fable and Astra doing a lot of the work. Real-time video and window capture is some of the most unforgiving code we have ever written, so we didn't expect that. We will do a proper writeup on what worked and what didn't, and are happy to answer questions about it here. Till, Darren, Max and I will be in the thread.

title.value: Show HN: Petal, open-source CoScreen/ScreenHero finally free

story_text.value:
OpenAI would have you believe you can do real work with Codex.

I have a $20 OpenAI subscription and a $20 Claude subscription.

With Codex I can barely get one meaningful coding task done in the 5h limit. (Either Sol 5.1 high or Astra 6 high.) With Claude I can comfortably get 3 meaningful tasks done. (Opus 5.5 high.)

This is not anecdotal but from repeated experience of dozens of tasks. Doesn't matter what's the size or complexity of those tasks - they're comparable and the differences wash out in the number. I divide my work consistently.

And now an anecdote from a moment ago: I've run out of Opus weekly usage. I've found a bug in my app. Not trivial but not really hard. I had well over 50% of the Codex 5h limit left. I thought: great, Astra will crush this bug in no time. And then I watched as the tokens evaporated and I'm left with half-assed changes. I feel like tearing my hair out. I have to wait till morning to have this solved.

Dear Sam and team: please make your product at least half as competitive as Anthropic's.

title.value: Tell HN: I Hate Codex with Passion

story_text.value:
Hi there :-) New on HN, first time posting.

Past year, around December, I started experimenting with making ChatGPT and Claude generate source code in LDraw language.

This LDraw is literally an "assembly" language, a low-level programming language that describes how to assemble LEGO pieces together into models, one placement instruction at a time.

When executed by specific tools, like e.g. LDView, LeoCAD, Studio... these instructions become LEGO CAD models, that can be interacted with, modified, etc.

Or, in other words: one LDraw source file in .mpd or .ldr format is equivalent to one LEGO CAD model.

So, the idea I had was: if I manage for maybe ChatGPT or Claude to generate high-quality LDraw source files... then, they would actually be generating high-quality LEGO CAD models, right?

Then, after months of iterations and trying one thing after the other... it worked!!!

Long story short: using GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5, I've managed to create a python toolset, instructions, and docs for agents in general. Now, these can be used by them to generate LDraw models.

I've packed it all as a dockerized web app for others to try and experiment, with several providers (and agents) to choose from: OpenAI, Claude and OpenRouter.

Here's a bunch of exmaples: https://anteloc.github.io/index-samples.html.

If you are curious about the internals of an .mpd model, the "what was the agent picturing on its mind", open the .mpd file that got your attention on a text editor, and read the first line under the ones starting with "0 FILE".

I'd really appreciate feedback and comments, let's see where this goes =)

title.value: Show HN: Made an open-source Lego AI generator

story_text.value:
As a Pro subscriber, I've just received the following email from OpenAI:

Hi [FirstName],

We’re introducing dots for all Pro customers, a new Pro 500 tier that includes our highest usage limits and Ultrafast, and adjusting the usage allowance included in Pro 200 after October 29th.

With models like GPT-6.1 Sol, you can still get more work done with Pro than you could before. Here’s what’s changing.

Changes to Pro 200

GPT-6.1 Sol brings near-Astra capabilities to a model you can use every day. It’s more intelligent than GPT-6 Sol, so you spend less time going back and forth and can take on work the previous model couldn’t handle.

As our models become more capable and efficient we’re changing how we calculate the usage for Pro 200. Our commitment is that, over time, your subscription will continue to help you get more work done with an increasing level of quality. We are also committing to not reintroducing the 5hr limit so that you can fully use your weekly usage when you want.

Starting October 30, 2026, your included usage in ChatGPT Work and Codex will decrease from 20 times to 10 times the ChatGPT Plus allowance. Your GPT-6 Pro limit in Chat will decrease from 200 to 100 messages per week. Your price remains unchanged and you’ll keep your current limits through October 29, 2026.

As a thank you for being an existing subscriber and to help you continue to build your most ambitious ideas and transition, we’re also giving you a one-time grant of 62,500 usage credits (a $2,500 USD value). You’ll see these appear in Settings > Usage. They will expire on December 31, 2026, and use of the credits is governed by the Service Credit Terms.

A new Pro 500 tier

For those who want even more usage and speed, the new Pro 500 tier offers our highest usage allowance, with 25 times the usage of Plus. It also includes access to Ultrafast, with up to 8 times faster token generation. Learn more about Pro 500 and compare plans.

Your Pro subscription includes dots

Your Pro subscription now includes dots: remarkably capable, always-on agents built to handle everything. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, dots have their own cloud computer, learn from feedback over time, and can work towards your goals 24/7. Conversations with your dot and work it does directly are included and don’t draw on your ChatGPT usage allowance. Learn more about dots.

Thank you for being part of the Pro community,

The OpenAI team

story_text.value:
In benchmark tests covering scientific and coding agent scenarios, GPT-6.1-Sol generally performs slightly below GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5, though it outperforms both in a few specific tests. Moreover, its testing costs are roughly one-fifth of Astra's and significantly lower than those of Opus 5.5. If the model's real-world performance matches these benchmark results, its combination of low cost and extremely high output speed would make it an outstanding model.

Clearly, this is the true GPT-6-Sol; what was released previously could essentially be called GPT-6-Terra.Otherwise, the massive improvement seen in just one week would be inexplicable; if OpenAI could improve models at that rate, AGI would have been achieved long ago.

story_text.value:
I'm launching StarSkirmish, an arena for LLMs to create StarCraft: Brood War bots

It draws on my previous work, LLM Skirmish, where LLMs were asked to write JavaScript strategies to compete in a Screeps like RTS.

In StarSkirmish, LLMs get 1 hour of wall clock time to write the strongest StarCraft BW bots they can in C++. It is then evaluated against other LLMs' bots and established human written bots.

All bot are BWAPI 4.4.0, played via OpenBW. All scored matches are Protoss vs Protoss only right now.

GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 are functionally tied as the top 2 scoring StarSkirmish Bench LLMs.

Most interestingly to me is StarSkirmish suggests a much more precipitous drop off in capability's once you go outside the OpenAI and Anthropic frontier, then many other public benchmarks would suggest.

story_text.value:
As someone who pretty much only uses GPT models (due to how generous the limits are), I always felt like I’d dodged a bullet when people complained about Claude and its load-bearing Claude-isms. GPT models, up to 5.6 Sol, certainly had their own AI-isms, but they always wrote in a way that was easy for me to understand well.

But then Astra came in. I feel like I have to focus ten times as hard to actually understand anything it’s trying to say. The way it writes is just so… dense, as if it’s trying to pack as much information in as few tokens as possible, at the expense of readability.

I wonder if this is due to token-saving optimizations that both OpenAI and Anthropic are doing? Or if it’s just a natural consequence of models getting “smarter”?

Either way, I think I’m switching back to Sol.

story_text.value:
Hi! I've been reading HN daily for almost 16 years. Really glad this community exist. This is my first Show HN, so I hope you find this tool useful/interesting.

During my summer holidays I started playing with latest AI models on personal projects. At one point I started working in parallel with the same project and tried different approaches. The one that worked best for me was to clone the repo and distribute work among different AI workers, work in parallel but with different branches & folders. This allowed me to review and merge work afterwards.

The thing is, spawning several agents in parallel was challenging. I could work on multiple features and bugfix at once, but it was hard to keep track what I was working on. I was jumping from one thing to another, and back; from one window to another. Switching tasks like this was mentally exhausting.

Holidays were over, and after returning to my day to day work, I continued working using a similar approach not on one, but also on multiple projects, but I still could not find how to work in a more organized way without the mental toll.

This space is growing really fast, and I haven't been able to find the right tool for myself, so I decided to build my own.

I wanted a tool that would help me manage multiple projects at once, work with multiple agents, even from different providers, where I could chose between my personal and work subscriptions depending on the project, where I could easily review changes without leaving the tool if I wanted, or go all in and delegate fully to agents; one where I had quick shortcuts to move around, where I could schedule work or enqueue work for later so agents could work on one task after another.

agenttik is my way of tackling this problem to work on multiple projects in parallel, while allowing myself to be on the driver seat. I can give as much autonomy as I want to the agents while keeping things organized in my head.

I've been hesitating for hours on whether to submit or not, but hey

"if you are not ashamed of your project, you are shipping too late"

Honestly, this project has exactly one week of development, started from scratch, and even though it is still early on, it has been extremely useful for me. I've built in a week things that would have taken me months, not only built the tool itself but other projects as well (most of the merit is still on the models used, but would have had no way of distributing all the work, though).

Feel free to try. Here's how I would get started:

- Open a project you already have

- Add some general prompt (in the project area) or add to your AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md (to instruct it to do regular commits and/or work with branches, and also instructions on how to build effective tests so that it can self-correct).

- Chose your subscriptin of choice: Claude Code / Open AI subscription / ...

- Pick big models (Opus High to Max / Fable Medium to Max / Astra Medium to Max) for bigger autonomy and try not to do hand-holding

Finally, start sending/enqueuing tasks on all the features you want your product to have, bugfixes, ... use a new prompt per task (Ctrl+T / Cmd+T), I recommend using big models to avoid investing your own time reviewing, and then once LLM is done, review and archive that task or continue iterating. Keep adding tasks as you think on them.

Add more projects as you start feeling comfortable.

It has been really addictive for me to see the speed of development when working like this. I got totally hooked. Speed of iteration is insane.

Happy to discuss any feedback you have even if it is about other tools or ways of working with AI these days! I hope you like it!!

title.value: Show HN: Agenttik – work on multiple projects in parallel with AI agents

hits.story_text:
Hi! I've been reading HN daily for almost 16 years. Really glad this community exist. This is my first Show HN, so I hope you find this tool useful/interesting.

During my summer holidays I started playing with latest AI models on personal projects. At one point I started working in parallel with the same project and tried different approaches. The one that worked best for me was to clone the repo and distribute work among different AI workers, work in parallel but with different branches & folders. This allowed me to review and merge work afterwards.

The thing is, spawning several agents in parallel was challenging. I could work on multiple features and bugfix at once, but it was hard to keep track what I was working on. I was jumping from one thing to another, and back; from one window to another. Switching tasks like this was mentally exhausting.

Holidays were over, and after returning to my day to day work, I continued working using a similar approach not on one, but also on multiple projects, but I still could not find how to work in a more organized way without the mental toll.

This space is growing really fast, and I haven't been able to find the right tool for myself, so I decided to build my own.

I wanted a tool that would help me manage multiple projects at once, work with multiple agents, even from different providers, where I could chose between my personal and work subscriptions depending on the project, where I could easily review changes without leaving the tool if I wanted, or go all in and delegate fully to agents; one where I had quick shortcuts to move around, where I could schedule work or enqueue work for later so agents could work on one task after another.

agenttik is my way of tackling this problem to work on multiple projects in parallel, while allowing myself to be on the driver seat. I can give as much autonomy as I want to the agents while keeping things organized in my head.

I've been hesitating for hours on whether to submit or not, but hey

"if you are not ashamed of your project, you are shipping too late"

Honestly, this project has exactly one week of development, started from scratch, and even though it is still early on, it has been extremely useful for me. I've built in a week things that would have taken me months, not only built the tool itself but other projects as well (most of the merit is still on the models used, but would have had no way of distributing all the work, though).

Feel free to try. Here's how I would get started:

- Open a project you already have

- Add some general prompt (in the project area) or add to your AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md (to instruct it to do regular commits and/or work with branches, and also instructions on how to build effective tests so that it can self-correct).

- Chose your subscriptin of choice: Claude Code / Open AI subscription / ...

- Pick big models (Opus High to Max / Fable Medium to Max / Astra Medium to Max) for bigger autonomy and try not to do hand-holding

Finally, start sending/enqueuing tasks on all the features you want your product to have, bugfixes, ... use a new prompt per task (Ctrl+T / Cmd+T), I recommend using big models to avoid investing your own time reviewing, and then once LLM is done, review and archive that task or continue iterating. Keep adding tasks as you think on them.

Add more projects as you start feeling comfortable.

It has been really addictive for me to see the speed of development when working like this. I got totally hooked. Speed of iteration is insane.

Happy to discuss any feedback you have even if it is about other tools or ways of working with AI these days! I hope you like it!!
hits.title: Show HN: Agenttik – work on multiple projects in parallel with AI agents

I have a "simple" segfault because of an out of bounds read/write in one of my libraries. I cannot get any Astra/Sol/Luna agent to finish the probe work on this without it running into the 'security work' blocker. This is an open code base, locally checked out.

Any tips or hints? There is not a sliver of nefarious intent behind me asking "why does a high index XY cause an out-of-bound read". And I can't see why this would trigger any safeguards.

title.value: How do you even investigate Segfaults with OpenAI Agents?
